mainTopic: Why the חכמים allowed business at the fair near עזה: comparing it to the case of two pots (a Jew's and a non-Jew's) cooking on one stove in צור, and the argument between אביי and רבא about what exactly the חכמים 'were not worried about.'
overview: This amud first finishes רבי חנינא's proof about the fair near עזה. He compares it to a case in צור, where a Jew and a non-Jew cooked two pots on one stove and the חכמים were not worried. Three אמוראים explain what the worry would have been. אביי says it was נבילה, which matches money of עבודה זרה. רבא says it was בישולי גוים, which matches business on יום אידם. רבה בר עולא says it was food splashing between the pots, which matches business in the days before the holiday. Next the גמרא turns to the משנה's line about traveling to a city celebrating a holiday, and brings a ברייתא where רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about it. The same ברייתא forbids bending down in front of an idol to remove a thorn, pick up coins, or drink from a spring, and forbids drinking from face-shaped fountains. The גמרא explains that 'if he is not seen' means 'if he does not look like he is bowing,' and shows why each of the three bending cases had to be taught.

steps.title: The two pots on one stove in צור
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא finishes his proof. In צור, a Jew and a non-Jew cooked two pots on one stove, and the חכמים were not worried.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Haven't you heard about the case in צור] where they put two pots on one stove? And the חכמים were not worried about it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a proof that רבי חנינא started just before this point. He brings the case of two pots on one shared stove, where the חכמים had no concern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forbidden food (the non-Jew's pot) sat right next to permitted food (the Jew's pot), and still the חכמים did not forbid it. רבי חנינא uses this to show that the חכמים were also not worried about the fair near עזה, even though it was close to a place of עבודה זרה.

keyTerms.meaning: they placed a pot on the fire
they were not worried / did not suspect a problem

phrases.english: that they placed two pots
phrases.notes: This finishes רבי חנינא's question, which started just before this point: 'Haven't you heard what we learned in צור...'

phrases.english: on top of one stove?
phrases.notes: One pot belonged to a Jew and one to a non-Jew.

phrases.english: And the Sages were not worried about them!

steps.triggerLanguage: ששפתו שתי קדירות על גבי כירה אחת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי חנינא's proof from the previous section about the fair of עזה.
steps.raayaObject: The חכמים were not worried about business at the fair near עזה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case in צור of two pots, a Jew's and a non-Jew's, on one stove, which the חכמים allowed.

steps.title: What were the חכמים not worried about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the חכמים were not worried about in the case of the pots.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'the חכמים were not worried about them' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. This sets up three different answers, from אביי, רבא, and רבה בר עולא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof only works if we know what the worry would have been in the pots case. Once we know that, we can see which worry about the fair near עזה it matches.

phrases.english: What is meant by 'the Sages were not worried about them'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the worry in step 1's case actually was.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which possible problem the חכמים chose to ignore in the two-pots case, and how it matches the fair near עזה.

steps.title: אביי: no worry about נבילה, so no worry about money of עבודה זרה
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the חכמים were not worried that the non-Jew would throw נבילה into the Jew's pot. In the same way, they were not worried about money of עבודה זרה at the fair.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We do not worry about נבילה meat. We do not say that maybe the Jew will turn his face around and the non-Jew will throw נבילה into his pot. In the same way, here too, the חכמים were not worried about money of עבודה זרה.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains that the worry in the pots case was that the non-Jew might secretly add non-kosher meat. He then applies this to the fair: the חכמים were not worried about money connected to עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both worries are about something forbidden by the Torah itself: eating נבילה, and money from עבודה זרה. אביי's point is that the חכמים did not forbid something just because a Torah problem might sneak in when no one is looking.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal that died without proper שחיטה; forbidden to eat
just like it / in the matching case

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Because of carcass meat, we do not say,
'Perhaps the Jew will turn his face around'
'and the non-Jew will throw carcass meat into the pot,'
just like that, here too
the Sages were not worried
about money of idol worship.
phrases.notes: He means the worry that money used for idol worship might end up in a Jew's hands at the fair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר אביי משום בשר נבילה לא אמרינן
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The worry was that נבילה might be added to the pot. Likewise, at the fair the חכמים ignored the worry about money of עבודה זרה.
steps.whyThisMatters: According to אביי, the חכמים were lenient even when the possible problem was a Torah prohibition.

steps.title: רבא: no worry about בישולי גוים, so no worry about יום אידם
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a different answer. The חכמים were not worried about בישולי גוים, and in the same way they were not worried about doing business on the non-Jews' holiday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What were the חכמים not worried about? בישולי גוים. In the same way, here too, the חכמים were not worried about their holiday (יום אידם).
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives another explanation of the pots case. The worry was that the non-Jew might cook the Jew's food. He matches this to the worry of doing business on the non-Jews' יום אידם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's worries are both rules of the חכמים, not Torah prohibitions: בישולי גוים, and doing business on יום אידם. So according to רבא, the leniency is only about rabbinic worries, while אביי allowed it even for a Torah worry like money of עבודה זרה.

keyTerms.meaning: food cooked by a non-Jew, forbidden by the חכמים
their (the non-Jews') holiday, when business with them is restricted

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two answers. אביי's worry (נבילה / money of עבודה זרה) is a Torah prohibition. רבא's worry (בישולי גוים / יום אידם) is only a rule of the חכמים.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי: the pots case shows no worry about נבילה, so no worry about money of עבודה זרה at the fair. רבא: the pots case shows no worry about בישולי גוים, so no worry about doing business on יום אידם.

phrases.english: Rava said:
What is 'the Sages were not worried about them'?
About food cooked by non-Jews.
Just like that, here too,
the Sages were not worried
about their holiday.

steps.triggerLanguage: רבא אמר מאי לא חשו להם חכמים משום בישולי גוים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to step 2's question than אביי gave in step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The worry was בישולי גוים. Likewise, at the fair the חכמים ignored the worry of doing business on יום אידם.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer limits the leniency to rabbinic worries, which changes how far the proof from the pots case reaches.

steps.title: רבה בר עולא: The worry was only about splashing
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר עולא says the חכמים were not worried about food splashing from the non-Jew's pot into the Jew's pot. In the same way, they were not worried about business in the days before the non-Jews' holiday.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר עולא said: The חכמים were not worried about splashing. Similarly here, the חכמים were not worried about the days before their holiday.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a third answer to the question in step 2. רבה בר עולא explains the pots case differently from אביי and רבא, and matches it to a milder situation at the fair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר עולא picks a very small worry: a drop of food might splash from one pot into the other. A drop like that is unlikely, and it would also be tiny compared to the Jew's food. So the matching case at the fair is also mild: business in the days before the holiday, not on the holiday itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Splashing; a drop of food spurting from one pot into another
Similar to it; the matching case
Before their holidays; the days leading up to the non-Jews' festival

steps.whatToRemember: There are three explanations of רבי חנינא's proof. אביי says the worry was נבילה and compares it to money of עבודה זרה. רבא says the worry was בישולי גוים and compares it to business on the holiday. רבה בר עולא says the worry was splashing and compares it to business before the holiday.
steps.confusionAlert: רבה בר עולא is not the same person as רבא from the previous step. Each of them gives a different answer.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Ulla said:
The Sages were not concerned
about splashing.
phrases.notes: He means a drop of food splashing from the non-Jew's pot into the Jew's pot.

phrases.english: Similarly, here too,
the Sages were not concerned
about the days before their holiday.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר עוּלָּא אָמַר: לֹא חַשּׁוּ לָהֶם חֲכָמִים מִשּׁוּם צִינּוֹרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third answer to the question in step 2, and an alternative to אביי and רבא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the חכמים were not worried about in the pots case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Splashing of food from pot to pot. It matches business before the non-Jews' holiday.

steps.title: Entering a city that has idol worship
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about traveling to a place with a holiday. It brings a ברייתא: רבי מאיר forbids entering or leaving such a city, and the חכמים forbid it only if the road leads only there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה asked what the law is about going there. A ברייתא teaches: In a city with idol worship, it is forbidden to enter it, or to go from it to another city. This is רבי מאיר's view. The חכמים say: if the road leads only to that place, it is forbidden. If the road does not lead only to that place, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, about going to a place celebrating a holiday. It brings a ברייתא with a מחלוקת on that topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר forbids entering such a city at all. He also forbids leaving it to travel on to another city. The חכמים look at the road instead. If the road goes only to that city, going there is forbidden. If the road also leads elsewhere, it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: A city where idol worship is taking place
A road that leads only to one place
And the Sages say; the opinion that disagrees

steps.whyThisMatters: The view of the חכמים matches the משנה's ruling. The question is whether the road shows where you are heading.

phrases.english: "What is the law about going there," etc.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the next line of our משנה, about traveling to a place celebrating a holiday.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A city in which there is idol worship:
it is forbidden to enter it,
and not to go from it to another city.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.
And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁהַדֶּרֶךְ מְיוּחֶדֶת לְאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם —
phrases.english: As long as the road leads only to that place,
it is forbidden.
If the road does not lead only to that place,
it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ לֵילֵךְ לְשָׁם וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר forbids entering or passing through a city with idol worship. The חכמים forbid it only when the road leads only to that city.

steps.title: Do not bend down in front of an idol
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. A person may not bend down in front of an idol to remove a thorn or pick up scattered coins, because he looks like he is bowing. If it does not look that way, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a thorn got stuck in a person's foot in front of an idol, he should not bend down and take it out, because he looks like he is bowing to the idol. If he does not look that way, it is permitted. If his coins scattered in front of an idol, he should not bend down and pick them up, because he looks like he is bowing to the idol. If he does not look that way, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא adds two cases about bending down in front of an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking out a thorn or picking up coins is not worship. It is forbidden only because of how it looks: bending in front of an idol looks like bowing to it. So when it does not look like bowing, it is allowed.
steps.whatToRemember: The ban here is about appearance. An innocent act is forbidden when it looks like bowing to an idol, and permitted when it does not.

phrases.english: If a thorn got stuck in him
in front of an idol,
he should not bend down and take it out,
because he looks like he is bowing to the idol.
But if he does not look that way, it is permitted.
If his coins scattered
in front of an idol,
he should not bend down and pick them up,
because he looks like he is bowing to the idol.
But if he does not look that way, it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָשַׁב לוֹ קוֹץ בִּפְנֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with more rules about acting near עבודה זרה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not bend down in front of an idol to remove a thorn or pick up coins, because it looks like bowing. If it does not look like bowing, it is permitted.

steps.title: Do not bend down to drink from a spring in front of an idol
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If a spring flows in front of an idol, a person may not bend down to drink, because he looks like he is bowing. If he does not look that way, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a spring flows in front of an idol, a person should not bend down and drink, because he looks like he is bowing to the idol. If he does not look that way, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from Step 7 continues with a third case: a spring of water flowing in front of an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is the same as for the thorn and the coins. Bending down in front of an idol looks like bowing, so it is forbidden. The גמרא asks what 'if he is not seen' means in Step 10 and answers it in Step 11.

phrases.english: A spring that flows in front of an idol —
one may not bend down and drink,
because he looks like he is bowing to the idol,
and if he is not seen — it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a third case of bending in front of an idol.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not bend down to drink from a spring in front of an idol, because it looks like bowing. If it does not look like bowing, it is permitted.

steps.title: Do not drink from fountain faces or straight from a pipe
steps.stepSummary: One may not put his mouth on a fountain shaped like a face, because it looks like kissing an idol. One also may not drink straight from a pipe, but that rule is because of danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: Statues with faces that spray water in the cities: a person should not put his mouth on their mouths and drink, because he looks like he is kissing an idol. In a similar way, he should not put his mouth on a pipe and drink, because of the danger.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a case about kissing instead of bowing. It then adds a pipe case that looks similar but has a different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Kissing an idol is also a kind of worship, so putting your mouth on a face-fountain looks like kissing it. The pipe case looks the same from the outside, but the reason is safety, not עבודה זרה.
steps.confusionAlert: The pipe rule is NOT about עבודה זרה. It is listed here only because it looks like the face case, and its reason is danger.

phrases.english: Faces that spray water in the cities —
phrases.notes: He means statues used as public fountains, with water coming out of the mouth.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַנִּיחַ פִּיו עַל פִּיהֶם וְיִשְׁתֶּה,
phrases.english: one may not put his mouth on their mouths and drink,
because he looks like he is kissing the idol.
Similarly —

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַנִּיחַ פִּיו עַל סִילוֹן וְיִשְׁתֶּה,
phrases.english: one may not put his mouth on a pipe and drink,
because of the danger.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a kissing case and a look-alike pipe case to the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not drink by putting his mouth on a face-fountain because it looks like kissing an idol, and one may not drink straight from a pipe because of danger.

steps.title: What does 'not seen' mean? It cannot mean nobody is watching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'if he is not seen' means. If it means nobody sees him, that contradicts רב's rule that something forbidden because of appearance is forbidden even in private.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'he is not seen' mean? If you say it means that nobody sees him, that is a problem. רב יהודה said in the name of רב: anything the חכמים forbade because of how it looks is forbidden even in the most private rooms!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the words 'if he is not seen' that the ברייתא repeats in Steps 7 and 8. It tries the simple meaning and shows that it does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple reading is that bending is fine when nobody is around. But רב taught that rules based on מראית העין apply even in total privacy. So 'not seen' cannot mean 'no one is watching.'

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion the גמרא is about to reject)
How something looks to others; forbidden because it looks wrong
In the innermost rooms, totally in private

steps.whyThisMatters: רב's rule is a major general principle: a rule made because of appearances still applies when nobody can see.

phrases.english: What does 'he is not seen' mean?
If you say that nobody sees him,
but didn't רב יהודה say in the name of רב:
Anywhere that the חכמים forbade something
because of how it looks,
it is forbidden even in the most private rooms!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אֵינוֹ נִרְאֶה אִילֵּימָא דְּלָא מִתְחֲזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the meaning of the last phrase of Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of 'if he is not seen' as 'if nobody is watching.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב said rules based on מראית העין apply even in private, so privacy cannot make it permitted.

steps.title: 'Not seen' means he does not look like he is bowing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: if he does not look like he is bowing to the idol, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say it this way: if he does not look like he is bowing to the idol, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by giving a new reading of the words 'not seen.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Not seen' is not about who is watching. It is about how the action looks: if he bends in a way that does not look like bowing, there is no problem at all, even in public.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (read the words this way)

phrases.english: Rather, say:
if he does not look like he is bowing
to the idol — it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from Step 10 by rereading the phrase.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the words of the ברייתא
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Not seen' means the action does not look like bowing.

steps.title: Why the thorn case alone is not enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the ברייתא needs several cases. From the thorn alone, we might think coins are permitted, since he cannot pick them up somewhere else.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is necessary to teach all the cases. If the ברייתא taught only the thorn, I would say it is forbidden because he can walk past the idol and take it out there. But the coins, where he cannot do that, I would say are not forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining why the ברייתא lists the thorn, the coins, and the spring, even though they seem the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thorn can wait until he walks past the idol, so being strict is easy. Coins stay where they fell, so we might think he is allowed to bend for them. That is why the coins had to be taught.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary (to teach every case)
Because if it had taught only
I would say it is not (forbidden)

phrases.english: And it is necessary, because if it taught only the thorn,
it is forbidden because he can walk further on and take it out,
but coins, where that is not possible —
I would say it is not forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the meaning of 'not seen' to why the ברייתא lists multiple cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The coin case is needed because the thorn case could be explained by the fact that he can remove the thorn elsewhere.

steps.title: Why the coins case alone is not enough
steps.stepSummary: From the coins alone, we might think it is only about money, and a thorn, which causes pain, would be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it taught only the coins, I would say it is forbidden because it is only money. But a thorn, which causes pain, I would say is not forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the other direction: the coin case alone would not teach us the thorn case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Losing money is less serious than being in pain. So we might think the חכמים would allow bending to remove a painful thorn. That is why the thorn had to be taught too.

phrases.english: And if it taught only the coins — that is because it is only money,
but a thorn, which causes pain — I would say it is not forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-way comparison between thorn and coins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The thorn case is needed because the coin case could be explained as only a money loss.

steps.title: Why the spring case is needed too, so all the cases are necessary
steps.stepSummary: From the thorn and coins, we might think that where life is at risk, like thirst, it is permitted. So the spring is needed, and all the cases are necessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it taught only these two, I would say they are forbidden because there is no danger. But a spring, where there is danger because if he does not drink he could die, I would say is not forbidden. So all of them are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes by explaining why the spring case was needed, and concludes that every case in the ברייתא teaches something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thorn and coins involve no danger to life. Thirst can be dangerous, so we might think bending to drink is allowed. The ברייתא teaches it is still forbidden if it looks like bowing.
steps.whatToRemember: Each case adds a new step: the coins are a case where he cannot wait, the thorn involves pain, and the spring involves danger. Even so, bending in front of an idol in a way that looks like bowing is forbidden in all of them.

phrases.english: And if it taught only these two —
that is because there is no danger,
but a spring, where there is danger,
because if he does not drink he could die —
I would say it is not forbidden.
So all the cases are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the third case and closes the צריכא discussion.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All three cases in the ברייתא are needed. Each one rules out a reason we might have used to allow bending in front of an idol.
